Almost every city on this route has a distinct character. Querétaro stands out for its aqueduct and Baroque architecture, San Miguel de Allende for its pink-stone streets and art galleries, Dolores Hidalgo for its role in Mexican independence, Guanajuato for its colourful buildings and Juárez Theatre, and Guadalajara for its cathedral, squares, Orozco murals and large city market.

## Cities along the route

The journey begins in Mexico City, the country’s cultural centre. The region brings together Aztec heritage, the colonial past and the life of a modern metropolis. Well-known places in and around the city include Teotihuacán, the Zócalo and Coyoacán.

Querétaro has a well-preserved historic centre inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Look for the arches of the aqueduct, colonial streets, churches and small cafés.

San Miguel de Allende is known for its pink-stone buildings, craft shops and art galleries. The Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel, with its distinctive Gothic façade, towers above the town centre.

Dolores Hidalgo is known as the cradle of Mexican independence. Here in 1810, Miguel Hidalgo called for an uprising against Spanish rule. The town is also known for its traditional pottery and local ice cream.

Guanajuato sits among hills and is distinguished by its narrow streets, colourful houses and underground roads. Its landmarks include the panoramic hill, the Mummy Museum and city squares where you can hear Mexican music.
